subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning a three.js module that assembles a chubby hedgehog from primitives, keeping within mesh, triangle, and color limits, using a seeded RNG and shared standard materials, sized roughly to a real hedgehog's proportions.

To stay efficient with mesh counts, I'm thinking I'll use InstancedMesh for the spines -- one instanced mesh for the brown bases and another for the cream tips -- rather than hundreds of individual cone meshes, which should keep the total mesh count well under the limit while still giving a dense, spiky coat look.

I'm sketching the body proportions as an ellipsoid with spines covering the upper hemisphere and sides, pointing outward with slight backward tilt and randomness. For the head, I'm planning a scaled sphere with a tapered cone-like snout extending forward to a pointed tip.

Now I'm working out facial details: fawn-colored head and snout, small dark beady eyes with tiny white catchlight highlights, a shiny black button nose at the snout tip with low roughness for a glossy look, tiny flattened round ears with pink inner discs at the sides of the head, and small pink paw ellipsoids positioned under the body front and back.

I'm nailing down the body proportions now, placing the body center and radius so the bottom sits just above the floor, with short legs barely peeking out and paws sized to touch the ground without sinking in. I'm also reconsidering overall height since adding spine length on top of the body makes the model taller than a realistic hedgehog, so I'm rescaling the body length and height to stay proportionate.

Now I'm starting to define the head dimensions and its position relative to the body, setting up the snout next.

I'm thinking through the snout shape as a forward-tilted cone with tiny whisker cylinders for a twitchy look. For spines, I'm figuring out how to sample points across the body's back and head crown, placing cone shapes pointing outward along the surface normals while avoiding the face region.

Working out the spine cone orientation and instancing...

With radialSegments at 5 and heightSegments at 1, each spine comes to about 15 triangles, so 260 spines plus similar tips keeps the total mesh count manageable. For placement, I'll sample roughly 320 points using golden-angle Fibonacci sphere distribution over the full sphere, then filter down to the upper ellipsoid region with seeded jitter for natural variation.

Now I'm working through the filtering logic: using 520 Fibonacci points, I need to exclude spines that fall inside the head ellipsoid zone near the front of the body (since the head would cover them), and also exclude points with downward-facing normals that would place spines on the belly rather than the back and sides.

For spine placement, I'm computing surface normals on the ellipsoid and tilting each spine's direction slightly backward with some random jitter for a natural, slightly swept-back look. Spine lengths will vary randomly between 0.028–0.040, with chestnut brown bodies and cream tips, and I'm considering using two brown shades across separate instanced meshes for visual depth.

Underneath the spines I need a dark chestnut body so there are no gaps, with a fawn-colored face and lighter fawn muzzle, darker fawn belly/legs, and pink paws using a standard material with moderate roughness. For the decorative leaf, I'm planning to build a maple leaf shape using a custom THREE.Shape outline with pointed lobes, then extrude it with a tiny depth for thickness in red material.

I'm now working out how to perch the leaf on top of the spines like a little trophy — positioning it near the upper back, slightly off-center, tilted so it rests convincingly on the spine tips with its stem pressed into them, along with a thin brown stem and a darker vein detail running through the leaf.

Now I'm figuring out the actual leaf shape — sketching a maple leaf as a hand-coded polygon outline with sharp-pointed lobes, scaled to about 8-9 cm across to look proportional against the hedgehog's body.

I'm abandoning the manual point-by-point approach in favor of a procedural method: generating the leaf outline as a polar curve with peaks at five lobe angles (top, upper sides, lower sides), with the stem positioned at the bottom, then sampling points around this curve to form the polygon.

The gap between the lower lobes naturally lands on the stem position, which works nicely. I worry the pure triangular shape will read as star-like rather than leaf-like, so I'm adding a subtle sinusoidal wobble to the radius for jagged serrated edges along each lobe, mimicking maple leaf teeth.

For the actual geometry, I'm generating the outline as a set of points sweeping around the full circle with 96 teeth, then extruding it with a thin depth and beveled edges, scaled down to realistic leaf size. I'll add veins as thin dark reddish boxes running from the center to each of the five lobe tips, layered slightly above the leaf surface.

I'm working out the rotation math so each vein box aligns with its lobe's angle in the leaf's local plane, then positioning a slim brown stem cylinder extending downward from the leaf base into the body's spine region, and placing the whole leaf group tilted at a slight offset position on the model.

I'm computing the leaf's full orientation quaternion: rotating about X by -π/2 makes the leaf's local Z axis map to world +Y (face-up), while checking how this rotation affects the leaf's local Y (top direction), which ends up pointing backward toward -Z, meaning the stem at the opposite end points forward.

Working out the yaw rotation so the leaf top angles forward-left, I'm applying Ry(b) to the already-flattened orientation to find the right combination that places the stem into the spine region while pointing the leaf's tip in the desired direction.

To get a natural dip, I decide to nest two groups: an outer group handling position, yaw, and tilt, with an inner leaf mesh carrying the flattening rotation, so the tilt applies in world space rather than the leaf's local plane.

Working through the leaf's stem geometry now, I realize the local rotation maps the stem direction forward instead of down into the spines, so I need to rework which local axis the stem extends along so it actually pierces downward into the cactus surface.

For simplicity, I'll keep the leaf lying flat on top with its stem tucked just slightly into the spines at the base, positioning the leaf center around (-0.02, 0.23, -0.05) to look like it's resting on the trophy of spines rather than literally impaled.

Now I'm working out head geometry: a fawn-colored ellipsoid head positioned above the body, plus a tapered snout made from a cylinder rotated to point forward, with its narrow tip facing +Z and its wider base nestled inside the head.

I'm placing a small black glossy nose sphere at the snout tip, calculating its exact coordinates from the cone's tip position and tilt angle. Now I'm working out where the eyes should sit on the sides of the head, verifying with the ellipsoid equation that the chosen position falls just inside the head surface.

I compute each eye's position using a surface-normal offset: pick a direction vector, project it onto the ellipsoid radii to get a surface point, then push outward slightly along the normal so the eye bulges naturally. This gives the right eye at roughly (0.042, 0.125, 0.17), with the left eye mirrored on the +X side, both rendered as small beady black spheres.

I'll give each eye a tiny white specular highlight sphere for that glossy, bright-eyed look. For the ears, I'm placing small flattened disc-shaped spheres on the upper sides of the head using the same surface-projection method, oriented to face outward along the local normal so they sit naturally against the head's curve.

I'm thinking fawn-colored outer ears with a smaller pink inner disc for contrast, and considering adding a few short spines along the crown behind the eyes so the spiky dome doesn't abruptly stop at bare skin.

For the crown spines, I need to carefully filter the placement so they don't overlap the ears or eyes — restricting to points with a steep upward normal and limited lateral spread near center. I'm also reconsidering the body-to-head boundary: excluding spine candidates that fall inside an expanded head ellipsoid so the two spine regions blend without collisions, though the front body spines mostly get filtered out this way.

Now I'm working out leg and paw placement, calculating body bottom heights at front and hind positions to position short cylindrical legs with pink paw ellipsoids beneath the body, keeping the visible leg length short like a real hedgehog's stubby limbs.

I'll skip adding a tail since hedgehogs have one hidden under the spines, and I'm deciding whether a belly patch is even needed given the dark body base color will mostly be hidden beneath the spine coverage anyway.

Now I'm working out spine distribution math: estimating body surface area to figure out spacing, settling on roughly 340 fibonacci-distributed candidate points filtered down to ~200 body spines plus ~30 head crown spines, using thin cones with low-poly radial segments. I'm setting up the fibonacci sphere distribution formula with jitter, then mapping those unit sphere points onto the ellipsoid body shape with proper normal calculation for spine orientation.

Defining spine tilt and rotation...

Then for the cream tip geometry, I'm placing its base slightly inset from the spine's apex, sizing its radius to roughly match the spine's taper point so it reads as a small cap rather than a jarring flange, nudging the exact ratios to avoid a visible step.

For the instanced meshes, I'm setting up separate instanced meshes for spines and tips with per-instance scale and color variation, keeping the brown spine tones subtly varied rather than flat.

For spine coloring, I'll use two distinct chestnut materials (dark and mid-tone) split randomly across instances rather than risky per-instance tinting, plus a cream tip color for contrast. For the overall look, I'm leaning toward flatShading with low segment counts to give the body and spines a faceted, low-poly feel while keeping the head ellipsoid smooth-ish at 16x12 segments.

I'm sketching out the full material palette now: chestnut tones for spines, cream for tips, fawn variants for face/head/belly/legs, pink for paws and inner ears, near-black for nose and eyes with a tiny white highlight sphere, plus leaf red/vein, stem brown, and a pale cream for whiskers. For whiskers, I'm thinking of using extremely thin cylinders fanning out from the snout, a few per side, to suggest that twitchy beady-eyed character detail even if they're subtle at distance.

For personality, I want to tilt the head slightly forward and give it a small yaw so it reads as alert, which means grouping all the head parts into a headGroup pivoted at the neck point so the rotation applies cleanly to everything at once.

I'm reconsidering though -- maybe skip rotating the head and rely on whisker twitch for charm instead, since head rotation complicates exclusion tests between head and body spines.

For the head group, I'm positioning it at the head's center and giving it a slight downward tilt and yaw so the snout dips and turns gently, working through how rotation order affects which way the nose points. Then I'm defining the head's local geometry -- ellipsoid radii and eye positions -- relative to that origin so the group transform carries them along automatically.

I'm working out the ear position locally, then checking the snout cone's placement: converting its world coordinates back to head-local space shows the cone's base sits mostly inside the head ellipsoid while the tip pokes out about 0.072 units past the front, giving a short, stubby snout rather than a sharply pointed one given the base radius.

Let me recompute the snout with a tilted cylinder axis instead — recalculating the base and tip positions accounting for the tilt angle confirms the base stays inside the head surface at z=0.04 while the tip extends to about z=0.15, and I'm now placing the nose slightly past the tip along that same axis.

For eyes, I'm testing a different direction vector that normalizes to push eye positions further forward on the head, landing around (0.037, 0.012, 0.050), which looks more front-facing than the earlier lateral placement.

I'm checking whether the eye sphere overlaps the snout base at this position and finding it's close but acceptable, then adjusting the direction vector again to push the eyes slightly outward to x≈0.047 so they clear the snout entirely.

Working through highlight placement for the eyes using an offset from the eye center along the normal plus an upward nudge, then mirroring it for the opposite eye. For the ears, I'm setting up position and orientation using a quaternion that aligns the flattened sphere's local z-axis to the surface normal, with a smaller pink inner-ear disk nested just above it.

Now I'm reconsidering the overall body proportions since my head and snout placement made the hedgehog too long nose-to-rump, so I'm redefining body and head centers/radii with cleaner numbers to bring total length down to around 32-35cm. I'm shifting to a code-based approach for the snout, ears, and eyes using axis vectors and ellipsoid-mapping functions rather than hand-computing world coordinates, which will also let me reuse the same logic for placing head-crown spines.

Writing spine placement logic...

I'm also working out leg, paw, and toe-bump placement under the body using the ellipsoid surface equation, confirming paws stay grounded and considering whether to give the pose a slight asymmetric stride, but deciding to keep a symmetric standing pose for clarity.

Writing spine instancing code...

I'm settling on using a seeded RNG for reproducible randomness and about to start writing the leaf shape generation function.

Writing maple leaf outline code...

Designing the serrated maple-leaf outline using lobe angles and triangular width functions, with a notch at the bottom where the stem attaches, and scaling the whole shape to roughly 4-4.5cm so it reads as proportionate to the hedgehog's body.

Writing leaf extrusion and vein code...
